title: The Stranger Who Loves You
speaker: Edward Espe Brown
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true fulfillment in Zen practice comes from cultivating a warm-hearted companion to oneself, rather than striving for external validation or perfection. This involves embracing all aspects of one's self, including difficult emotions and experiences, with kindness and acceptance. By doing so, we can find inner peace and connection with others, and let go of the need to change or fix ourselves in order to be worthy.

*You will love again the stranger who was yourself.
Give wine, give bread.
Give back your heart to itself, to the stranger who's loved you all your life, whom you ignored for another, who knows you by heart.
Take down the photographs from the bookcase.
Take back the desperate notes.

Feast.

Pretty tasty tonight, or?
Suzuki Roshi told us one time about when he was practicing with Gyokujun So-on, Roshi.
He was a young man.
I think he went when he was 11.
So somewhere at 11, 12, 13, 14, this happened.
They would make pickled daikon.
We used to do it at Tassajara, back in the day.
We had big barrels, and you'd layer the radishes and the cabbage and all in with the rice bran and then salt, rice bran and salt.
The salt dries the water out of the vegetables and the rice bran flavors them a little bit.
One year they didn't put enough salt in, and the pickles, instead of getting pickled, rotted.
I've been around some pickles like that.
It's what we call a barnyard aroma.
It has very much this kind of aroma.
We threw them out at Tassajara.
But Suzuki Roshi's teacher Gyokujun So-on said they would eat them, because in Zen you do not waste food.
He called this food.
So these young men weren't interested in eating rotten pickles.
They would eat other things instead of the pickles, and the teacher kept serving them.
Then one night young Suzuki Roshi took the pickles to the far end of the garden, dug a hole and buried them.
Thinking, isn't that the way to handle something that's distasteful?
Isn't that what we've all done with our distasteful experiences, especially from very early, when we didn't have other skills and tools for handling what was distasteful?
The hole is usually inside you then, and you bury it somewhere.
It's called repression, or childhood trauma that you tuck away someplace.
Anyway, we don't need to go there.
We don't want to.
The next morning the pickles were on the table again.
He didn't want to know who had buried them.
He just said, "We're eating these pickles before we eat anything else."
So they sat down and started eating pickles.
Suzuki Roshi said it was a very, very important experience in his life.
He said it was the first time he experienced what is called in Zen "no thought."
Chew and swallow.
Because if you think anything, you would have to spit them out.
This is terrible.
I hate this.
This is horrible.
If you think anything, you can't do it.
So perhaps some of you tonight, sitting, greet yourself arriving at your own door, in your own mirror.
Rotten pickles.
Over the course of time, you will have many different meals of zazen.
It can't be helped.
I can't tell whether it's too many years or not enough years of Zen: 20 years of living at Zen Center and 50 or 80 sesshins and 15 or 16 practice periods.
Now you need one practice period and one sesshin and then you can have Dharma transmission and become a member of the Soto Zen Teachers of America.
Easy.
And you probably don't even have to eat any rotten pickles.
You can eat half peanut butter sandwiches instead.
But then I did Vipassana practice, and one year I was at IMS in Barre, Massachusetts.
It's a three-month retreat, like a practice period, but it's Vipassana.
So there's no talking, and you write notes to people if you want to.
Then you get to talk to your teacher for 10 minutes every other day, one of your teachers.
So, like a practice period.
Right before the last 10 days, one of the teachers, Joseph Goldstein as a matter of fact, said, "Many people do 10-day retreats or week-long retreats, two-week retreats.
You've now had two and a half months of retreat to prepare for these last 10 days.
So we could call this dessert."
You've practiced and practiced and now you have 10 days.
This is the way it is if you practice for 90 days and then end with the sesshin.
During the last 10 days I went to see Joseph, and he asked me what I'd been noting, because you practice noting in Vipassana.
I said I'd been noting disgust, distaste, abhorrence, a lot of it.
It doesn't taste like dessert to me.
And Joseph said, "It may not be the dessert you ordered.
But it's the dessert that's being served."
You might think that practice is about getting better meals, better experiences.
But if you've been a cook, you know that some meals come out better and some don't.
Some come out worse.
Of course, when you're the cook, you understand: you're only as good as your last meal.
So it's very stressful to be the cook because you said surpass, yes.
And then people at Tassajara, when I was a cook, would come up to me and say, "That was really good.
How are you going to surpass yourself tomorrow?"
They actually ask you that.
And you can't.
You can't surpass yourself.
But you're only as good as your last performance.
You're only as good as your last asana.
How's it going?
How good are you tonight?
Greet yourself arriving at your own door.
Give wine, give bread, give back your heart to itself.
Or did something else happen?
Oh well, it's not the dessert you ordered.
So what are we going to do?
Do we set out to see how we ensure that we get the proper service around here?
Yo, body, yo, mind, thoughts, feelings.
Come on now, get it together.
I want something better than this tonight.
We'd better be good, make it good.
Do you tell yourself that?
Or do you say, "Sweetheart, whatever you have to share with me, I'm here for you"?
Not very many of us have that kind of interpersonal skills or intrapersonal skills.
"Sweetheart, anything you want to share with me, I'm here.
I'm going to sit with you for the next half hour, 40 minutes.
Let me know what's on your mind, what's in your heart.
What's your aesthetic tonight?
What's up?"
And most of the time: oh, no, not that.
I don't want to hear about that.
So is it important to get good results?
Or is it important to be a warm-hearted companion to someone who's...
Whose idea was this?
That's what Rumi says: whose idea was this, to get born in this world?
All in all, it's probably not so bad, huh?
But I have the feeling that out in the Bardo, they have advertisements that are kind of like new car ads.
Do you know in a new car ad, you cruise in your car?
Is there any traffic in new car ads?
You just cruise down these country roads and there's nobody in front of you going along 15 miles an hour under the speed limit.
When you cruise into the city or you go across the bridge, there's plenty of room.
It's not like I-5 going in during the commute time.
I'm going four miles to the train station next Monday, and the woman at Nalanda West said, "Your train is at 7:25."
Well, we're going to have to leave at 5:30.
But out in the Bardo, you cruise in your new car, pull up to the train station and just park.
There's plenty of parking.
It's easy.
You don't even have to parallel park.
You just pull into the curb and stop, and probably somebody opens the door for you.
So you think, oh, what a life.
And then they're saying in the Bardo, "Get a life.
Get a life."
Then you get here and you're like, what was I thinking?
I can't even sit here with myself and count on a warm-hearted, friendly experience unless I provide it.
And it's always up to me.
It's never up to the other.
I have to be, oh, I have to be the adult around here?
Oh, gosh.
I was hoping that if I behaved well enough, some adult would show up and tell me what a great sweetheart I was, because I'm finally behaving well enough.
And I've calmed my mind and eliminated the hindrances and the afflictive emotions and the, what are those called?
Oh, the kleshas, the kleshas.
One year I got a job for three weeks teaching cooking.
That's actually how I got here, come to think of it.
I got a job teaching cooking for three weeks at Karme Choling, Trungpa Rinpoche's center in Barnett, Vermont.
That's where I met Paul and Jenny Warwick, who then said, "Come to Bellingham."
They lived here.
Yeah.
Well, it's been 20 years, so wouldn't you suppose?
So I went to work there, and the day I got there, they said, "Oh, you missed a great experience this morning."
We only have the newest people working in the kitchen, because as you become more senior, you only do spiritual practice.
You meditate and you do a hundred thousand prostrations and a hundred thousand incantations and a hundred thousand, you have five hundred thousands.
They don't count cutting onions.
Cut your hundred thousand onions.
That doesn't count.
Even if you cry while you're cutting onions, it doesn't count.
You have to do the authorized things that are counted as spiritual practice.
The unauthorized things like working in the kitchen and cutting onions and carrots and celery and washing pots, that doesn't count.
Which is really different than Zen style, right?
Because we say only the most senior people work in the kitchen.
That's not quite true, but it's in the literature, whether it's in practice or not.
So there they say, well, we only have the newest people because the other people, as they become more senior, are making statues of deities out of butter, butter statues of deities.
They're visualizing Chakrasamvara and Vajrasamadhi or whoever.
And that's spiritual practice, but the kitchen, no.
So the new people were in the kitchen and they were going to make scrambled eggs for 300 people.
Or it was 300 eggs maybe, for 100 people.
They thought, this is going to be a lot of work to crack the eggs one by one.
Why don't we just put all the eggs in the Hobart mixer, turn it on, and then strain the egg out of the shell?
They found out it doesn't work.
So they had this massive bowl of eggs and shells that they had to throw away.
One thing led to another, and little by little I became familiarized with this place and how it works.
I would go into work and nobody else would show up.
Maybe half an hour later somebody would come in.
After a couple of hours maybe somebody would come by and say, "Jean's not coming to work today.
She's having a klesha attack."
Apparently that was a good reason not to work.
If you didn't feel like working, you didn't have to work.
That's what a klesha attack was: if you're feeling sad or scared or helpless or vulnerable in some way, fragile, you just don't go to work.
And this is after years of training myself: if you feel sad, you bring it to the kitchen with you and you put it to work with you.
You start to cry and your tears fall into the food or into the sink, into the soapy water.
If you're feeling angry, then wash some pots, cut some food.
You put the anger to work.
You don't say, "When I go to work in the kitchen, we're just going to have a spiritual time, and it's going to be very sweet and mellow.
So we can't have this anger stuff around here.
When we cook, we have to be perfectly loving.
So you're not allowed to come in the kitchen with me.
You better stay outside here."
Then how do you get any work done?
So my idea, which I learned pretty early on, because in Zen when the bell rings to go to work or the drum hits to go to work, you go to work.
It doesn't matter whether you have a klesha attack or not.
You bring it with you and you say, "Sweetheart, I know you're upset right now, but help me out here.
See what you can do with these carrots and these onions and the celery and the things we have to clean up and wash and all of that.
Come on.
It's a little bit like, I'm sorry.
As you can tell, I didn't figure out this talk ahead of time.
I told Marjorie this morning, "Oh, great, I'm giving a talk in Billingham.
Oh, I can give you the same talk I gave at the Seattle Soto Zen last night."
And it's just not happening.
It's not always the same.
But at some point I may switch over and give you the talk from last night.
You'll tell.
This is like one of my dear students who lives a couple blocks away.
She and her husband are both artists, and they have a big studio building, which used to be Carl's Studio, and now my partner, Marjorie, is a part of that for her painting studio.
So I've known Marie now since about 1996, 20 years now.
Anyway, her husband died.
He was a metal sculptor, and his lungs gave out.
Apparently he was not careful enough about wearing masks when you do welding on metal sculpture.
There are volatile metals in the air, and you start breathing them in, and then they cool down in your lungs and turn back to metal, so his lungs were full of metal.
And we chanted what we chanted just now, the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, while he was passing.
And I did the memorial service.
Then Marie was just distraught and devastated.
I would go over, and I was doing grief counseling with her.
The classic kind of grief counseling is not so unlike sitting zazen, greet yourself arriving at your own door and your own mirror.
You make a list, and you start from the earliest you can remember.
What happened when you were in the womb?
What happened when you were born?
What happened when you were a baby?
Because any grief today opens up all the grief of your life.
And mostly in your life, people have said, "Oh, don't be sad.
Don't be upset.
We'll get you another cat.
Don't be sad.
Don't be scared.
Don't cry.
Don't grow up."
So most of us didn't have a chance through all these times in our life.
We just never had a chance to grieve.
So when something happens today, if you have the chance...
I was fortunate at one point to have a friend of mine come over.
She came over seven times for about two hours each.
You don't even remember how painful it was until you start talking about it.
But I'm not going to bore you with the painfulness in my life, except for one thing that I didn't realize at all.
I found out when I was talking to her that I went to six different grammar schools.
I wasn't thinking about that.
And then she said, "Well, did you have friends?
Did you have sleepovers?"
No.
Well, who did I know?
It's new kids every year.
And then you can cry and sob, and there's somebody there with you.
And then after a while she says, "And you survived that, didn't you?
You survived that."

So that you survived that is the more you can bring to mind: not the person who was upset and hurt and grieving, but the person who survived that, who was so strong and so determined and so courageous to be in this world and to survive and to go on with this life.
That's you.
And that's still who you are and why you're here and not out at the bar or a lot of the other places you might be.
This, by the way, goes along a little bit with...
I have to come back to Marie.
I'm aware of that.
So if I don't come back to Marie, all right, I'll come back to Marie and then we'll go on to my other point.
But then I might forget my other point.
I have to tell you this before I forget all about it.
Now that I'm a Sounds True author, with my book *No Recipe*, I'm on their email list, so I get these things.
They have a summit on [unclear: "spiritual audience psychology"] and they have 20 speakers over three days, and for 24 hours you can listen free, and then you have to pay to listen.
But since I'm a Sounds True author, they just download it onto my account.
So I was listening to, I think it was, James Hollis, who's a psychotherapist in Washington D.C., and he said sometimes you might want to sit down with your inner critic, your judge.
The person who's saying, "You call that zazen?
Are you still getting upset and disturbed?
Can't you concentrate any better than that?
What's wrong with you anyway?"
There's some voice in you that's pretty judgmental and harsh and critical, and it's going to straighten you out.
And you say, "Thank you.
I really benefited from your being here, because when I was three or four and you showed up, I didn't know what to do and you told me.
So you got me through a lot.
So how old do you think I am today?"
I asked my inner critic and he said, "Well, seven."
Your critic's been so busy looking for what you did right and what you did wrong, it's not noticing that you're growing up.
It's got a very limited frame of mind.
So it's up to you to enlighten this person.
"How old do you think I am?
I'm 73 now, and you might be willing to talk to me a little bit differently, like I'm an adult and not like I'm a kid who needs to be shamed into behaving properly.
I mean, get over it.
And be a little polite if you have something to tell me.
Instead of saying, 'What's wrong with you and why can't you?' you might consider, and here's something that you could think about and take to heart."
You might want to take it to heart, but you'll see.
I'll offer it to you.
So you can change your relationship with this entity, or whatever aspect of yourself that is busy.
And then how do you sit with yourself and greet yourself arriving at your own door?
That's not the way to do it.
That's not how you greet yourself arriving.
Well, not if you're here.
Get out of here.
Of course I can't greet anybody arriving when you're showing up.
Anyway, so Marie.
This went on for a number of months, and then after about ten months I started giving her books.
I gave her a copy of the Grief Recovery book, which is a great book, James and Freeman or somebody.
And then I gave her Susan Piver's book that just came out, about the wisdom of a broken heart.
In Susan's book she says that in any relationship you're taking a vow to have your heart broken sooner or later.
Mostly, of course, it's sooner.
You get divorced.
But sometimes it's later, when your partner dies.
Or when you say, "I'm leaving now.
I thought I would always be here for you, but it doesn't look like it."
So Marie read Susan's book and she said, "That was a good book, Ed.
It had a lot of interesting exercises in it.
None of them work."
But it's interesting, because she read the book and then about ten days, two weeks later she called me and she said, "Ed, I realize it's up to me to take care of myself.
Marie, I say to myself, 'Marie, I know you don't feel like doing a thing.
Let's get you something to eat.
Marie, I know you're depressed.
Let's get you outside for a walk.'" She said, "I realize I'm going to just have to take myself in hand.
Nobody else has got the job.
Nobody else is doing this."

So we have this awesome, awesome task [unclear: "in Susan"] to be here and listen to ourselves, be here with ourselves and be willing to hear and receive all the grief, all the sorrow, all the rage, all the abandonment, the betrayals.
Most of us have been betrayed, some more seriously than others.
And we've all been abandoned.
But then, of course, you start to study.
Okay, I'll tell you a little piece of my life.
When I was three, my mother died.
It was two weeks after my third birthday.
Coincidentally, it's a date that is well known in Zen.
We often celebrate it as Buddha's birthday, April the 8th.
I forgot that my mother had died that day, but every April the 8th, people are going around saying, "Happy birthday, Buddha.
We're all Buddha.
Happy birthday, Buddha."
And I'm like, "F you too."
And then finally, after 30 years at the Zen Center, I said, at Green Gulch one day and I said, "Oh, it's April the 8th.
It's the day my mom died."
So, did she abandon me?
What was she thinking, to go and die like that?
She didn't want to.
It wasn't her choosing.
She desperately wanted to be here for her kids, my brother and me.
And what about me?
What does that say about me?
I was not good enough.
I was not competent enough.
If I'd been better at being a human being, if I'd behaved better, she wouldn't have died like that.
She wouldn't have gone away.
She would have stayed here, if I had behaved better.
Is that true?
So we come up with all these stories.
And what Buddhism says is you come up with all these stories and then you settle down on the stories and forget that you just made it up.
And then you wonder how to fix the story rather than making a new one, dispelling that story and making of the new story the story of today, the story of tonight, the story of now.
So William Stafford has a poem.
Do you know William Stafford?
He was an Oregonian.
Is it Oregon?
Or is he a Washington?
Oregon, yeah. [unclear: "Oregon Sisters"].
And the most well-known story about him is that he wrote a poem every day.
Once he was interviewed and the woman said, "Your friend Robert Bly says you write a poem every day."
He says, "Yes, I get up in the morning and I start in on the poem, and then I have to stop and get the kids up, get them breakfast, get them off to school.
Yeah, and then I take it down, and I have a shelf to keep the poem, and if I can I work on it during the day, and if not I finish it at night before I go to sleep."
And the woman doing the interview said, "Mr.
Stafford, how can you do that?
How can you write a poem day in and day out?
I mean, to be that creative, this would be like sitting in sesshin every day, for goodness' sakes.
How could you do that every day?"
And he said, "I lower my standards."
So, anyway, one of his shorter poems, maybe he lowered his standards, but it's a pretty good poem.
*It could happen any time.
Earthquake, tornado, Armageddon.
It could happen or sunshine, love, salvation.
It could.*
That's why we wake up and look out.
There are no guarantees in this life.
But there are some, he called it bonuses, but I usually say blessings, some blessings like morning, like noon, like night, like right now.
So which story will it be?
Okay, one Zen story and we'll finish.
Do you know the two monks were walking along?
And one of them said, "Right here, this is the summit of the Mystic Peak.
What do you think?
Here?
Tonight?
No?
This is the summit of the Mystic Peak."
And the other one was a little in that William Stafford mode.
"Yes, indeed.
Isn't it a pity?
Because who thought it would be better than this?"
So, of course, anyway, there's commentary on these things.
The commentary basically says, did you know that at the summit of the Mystic Peak there's weeds?
Some of them are six foot tall, some of them are twelve.
At the summit of the Mystic Peak, you could get lost in the weeds.
But anyway, the best commentary is, once a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Master, how can I get to the summit of the Mystic Peak?"
And Zhaozhou said, "I'm not sane.
I won't tell you."
If you've read up in your Zen history, you know that when Zhaozhou spoke, golden light came out of his mouth.
That's what it says.
So why wouldn't you say anything?
So the monk, of course, has the same question that we have.
"Why won't you tell me?" the monk asked him.
And Zhaozhou said, "If I said anything, you'd go right on thinking that right now you were still on level ground."
How is it that you think that?
We're spinning a story and then we settle down in it, and then we wonder, like, how do I fix this?
Marie?
I know you don't feel like doing anything.
Let's get you out for a walk.
Let's get you a cup of tea.
*Greet yourself arriving at your own door.
Sit here, eat.
You will love again the stranger who was yourself, whom you ignored by another who knows you by heart.*
May our intentions equally extend.
